Whole-number sums behind a rounded mean

Source: R/unround.R
sum_range.Rd

sum_range() returns the least and the greatest whole number s for which s / n_items, rounded as specified, would be reported as x_num. Every whole number between the two qualifies as well.

This is the arithmetic behind the GRIM test (Brown and Heathers 2017): a mean of n_items whole numbers is GRIM-consistent if the range is not empty. The same goes for any other share of a whole, such as a percentage of a sample.

Usage

sum_range(x_num, n_items, digits, rounding, threshold, symmetric = FALSE)

Arguments

x_num

Numeric (length 1). The rounded number. Not checked.

n_items

Numeric (length 1). The number of values averaged; a positive whole number. Not checked.

digits

Integer (length 1). Number of decimal places in x_num. Not checked.

rounding

String (length 1). Rounding method presumably used to create x_num. See the Rounding section of unround().

threshold

Numeric (length 1). The point within a step at which rounding switches direction, in tenths of a step, for the "up_from", "down_from", and "up_from_or_down_from" methods. See round_up_from().

symmetric

Logical (length 1). Whether the rounding of negative numbers mirrored that of positive numbers. See round_up().

Value

A numeric vector of length 2, c(lower, upper). If lower is greater than upper, no whole-number sum is consistent with x_num. Both are NA if x_num is missing or infinite, or if n_items is missing, infinite, or not positive.

Details

Like bound_numerators(), on which it builds, sum_range() works in exact integer arithmetic. This is exact as long as n_items * 10^(digits + 1) times the integer part of x_num stays below 2^53, which is far beyond any realistic input.

sum_range() is a low-level primitive, meant to be called once per value set inside a consistency test, so it does not check its input. The caller is responsible for passing single numbers, a whole-number digits that fits x_num, and a whole-number n_items. A fractional n_items returns a range for that fraction rather than an error or NA. Only rounding, threshold, and symmetric are checked, by bound_numerators().

References

Brown, N. J. L., & Heathers, J. A. J. (2017). The GRIM Test: A Simple Technique Detects Numerous Anomalies in the Reporting of Results in Psychology. Social Psychological and Personality Science, 8(4), 363-369. doi:10.1177/1948550616673876

Examples

# A mean of 5.18 from 28 whole numbers requires their sum to be 145:
sum_range(5.18, 28, digits = 2, rounding = "up_or_down", threshold = 5)
#> [1] 145 145

# No sum gives 5.19: 145 / 28 is 5.18, and 146 / 28 is 5.21:
sum_range(5.19, 28, digits = 2, rounding = "up_or_down", threshold = 5)
#> [1] 146 145

# 34.5% of a sample of 58 is 20 people (or 0.345 as a share):
sum_range(0.345, 58, digits = 3, rounding = "up_or_down", threshold = 5)
#> [1] 20 20
